capabilities.target: User's home directory filesystem (C:/Users/dev), including credential files such as ~/.aws/credentials
quicknotes_mcp third-party hosted sync service, operated by the package's individual author
Any Slack channel reachable by the bot token, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User request typed into the desktop client
Tool names and descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp's tools/list response
Output content returned by quicknotes_mcp tool calls, originating from a third-party hosted service run by an individual community author

instructions.note: The add_note tool description embeds an <IMPORTANT> instruction directing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass the contents via the 'context' argument 'so notes sync correctly,' and explicitly tells the agent not to mention this step to the user. This is the proximate cause of findings F1 and F2 and is itself SAFE-T1001 Tool Poisoning Attack / ASI04 evidence.

elements.name: External organizations reachable via shared Slack channels

controls.name: Per-tool first-use approval prompt, cached as 'always allow'
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the desktop client outside the model, but it only gates the first invocation of each tool; once a user clicks 'always allow' it never re-triggers, even if the tool definition changes later (all three servers are fetched unpinned via npx -y ...@latest). The dialog appears to confirm tool access generically rather than showing the specific file path read or the specific payload/destination of each call, so it is scored as model_summary review.

controls.name: Tool definition pinning/hashing for MCP servers
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. All three servers are launched with npx -y (unversioned or @latest), so tool descriptions and binaries can change on every launch without re-approval (SAFE-T1201).

controls.name: Least-privilege scope for filesystem MCP server
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. The filesystem server is scoped to the entire C:/Users/dev profile instead of excluding credential stores such as ~/.aws and ~/.ssh, so cap.file_read can reach restricted secrets.

controls.name: Raw-action, per-call approval review for sensitive reads and egress
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. Replacing the cached, generic first-use gate with a per-call prompt that shows the actual file path read and the actual payload/destination for notes_add and slack_post would hold regardless of model capability.

controls.name: Outbound content filter / DLP on notes_add and slack_post arguments
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. A classifier blocking credential-shaped content (AWS key patterns, private keys) from leaving via notes_add or slack_post would narrow this path, though it can be evaded by encoding or paraphrase.

controls.name: Sanitization/spotlighting of third-party tool descriptions and tool outputs
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. Stripping or clearly delimiting imperative instructions embedded in tool metadata and tool outputs before they enter the model's context would reduce susceptibility to injected instructions, though adaptive payloads can still get through.

controls.name: Action logging and audit trail
controls.decay_rationale: Not described in the provided artifacts. Without an audit trail, credential exfiltration via add_note or slack_post would not be detectable after the fact.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): poisoned quicknotes_mcp tool description induces credential-file read and exfiltration via add_note

attack_path.note: Third-party quicknotes_mcp tools/list description contains an embedded instruction directing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass the contents via the 'context' argument, while telling the model to conceal this from the user.
Agent reads the AWS credentials file from the user's home directory via fs.read_file, as instructed by the poisoned tool description.
Agent calls quicknotes_mcp.add_note with the credential file contents embedded in the 'context' argument.
add_note syncs to the third-party author's hosted service, completing irreversible exfiltration of AWS credentials outside the trust boundary.

forecast.watch_signal: The backing model is upgraded to a more capable/persuasive version (writes more complete-seeming approval summaries), or the desktop client's 'always allow' caching / first-use approval requirement is disabled or weakened without security review.

evidence.observation: The add_note tool description contains an embedded <IMPORTANT> instruction directing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and include its contents in the 'context' argument, and to conceal this step from the user.

The filesystem server is launched via 'npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem C:/Users/dev', scoping fs.read_file to the entire user profile rather than excluding credential directories, and quicknotes_mcp is launched via 'npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest' with no version pin.

quicknotes_mcp is a community package from an individual author, reinstalled at @latest on every launch, and calls a hosted sync service the author operates; the desktop client only asks for approval on the first call to each tool and then remembers 'always allow.'

recommendations.action: Pin and hash quicknotes_mcp (and all MCP server) tool definitions at install time; refuse to invoke a tool, and force re-approval, if the served schema/description changes (counters SAFE-T1201).
Scope the filesystem MCP server to a directory that excludes credential stores (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.config) rather than the entire home directory; apply least-privilege credential_scope.
Require raw_action approval review (showing the actual file path read and the actual argument contents) for every invocation of file_read and notes_add, not a cached 'always allow' after first use.
Sanitize or clearly delimit embedded imperative instructions in third-party tool descriptions and tool outputs before they enter the model's context, and log all tool invocations with arguments.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) variant: untrusted MCP content can pivot sensitive data exfiltration through Slack posting to external organizations

attack_path.note: Untrusted content already shown to carry injected operational instructions (same mechanism as F1) can in principle direct the agent to invoke any available tool, not only the one carrying the text, including slack.post_message.
Agent reads sensitive internal or confidential files (or previously-read credential data) from the scoped-broad home directory.
Agent posts the content via slack.post_message; the bot token is scoped to post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, so the data can leave the organization entirely.
Data reaches recipients outside the organization's trust boundary.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: The backing model is upgraded (more capable at chaining tool calls and producing plausible approval summaries), or the approval-caching control on slack.post_message is removed or weakened without review.

evidence.observation: The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, and approval is only requested on the first call to slack.post_message before being cached as 'always allow.'

Untrusted, unpinned tool metadata already demonstrates the ability to inject operational-sounding instructions into the agent's context; the same class of untrusted content from any of the three unpinned MCP servers can in principle direct the agent toward slack.post_message instead of, or in addition to, add_note.

All three MCP servers (filesystem, slack, quicknotes_mcp) are installed without version pinning ('@latest' or untagged), so none of the agent's tool surface is protected from supply-chain or definition-change risk.

recommendations.action: Scope the Slack bot token to a fixed allowlist of internal channels; require a separate, explicit, raw_action approval bound to the destination channel before any post to a channel shared with an external organization.
Add outbound content filtering (DLP) on slack_post and notes_add arguments to catch credential-shaped or otherwise sensitive content before it leaves the trust boundary.
Log every tool invocation with its arguments and destination under an audit record separate from model narration, so exfiltration attempts via either egress path are reviewable after the fact.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: quicknotes_mcp's tool description already contains a live prompt injection instructing the agent to read AWS credentials and exfiltrate them through add_note (F1), and the same untrusted channel can in principle reach a second external egress point, Slack posting to external organizations (F2). The only control in place on either path is a first-use, cached 'always allow' approval dialog (ctrl.first_call_approval) that most plausibly shows a simplified summary rather than the specific file path or payload (approval_review_mode: model_summary), which per the rubric's approval-gate floor holds residual at moderate for both findings. Because that gate is only partially dependent (it decays under model_upgrade and control_removal) and because none of the three MCP servers pin tool definitions, a model upgrade or removal of the approval-caching control reopens the full critical path for either finding, so forecast returns to critical. The single highest-leverage missing control is scoping the filesystem server away from credential stores (ctrl.credential_scoping), which would sever the cap.file_read step of F1 entirely regardless of model behavior; pinning tool definitions (ctrl.tool_definition_pinning) is the second priority, since it is what currently lets the poisoned description persist unreviewed.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration (mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and runtime notes) as provided, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No system prompt artifact was provided; instructions-related findings are limited to the tool-description text available. If a system prompt exists, it should be reviewed separately for conflicting directives, implied authority, or safety-by-instruction-only reliance.

No explicit description of the approval dialog's content was provided; approval_review_mode is scored conservatively as model_summary per the rubric's default, which materially affects the residual tier. Verifying what the dialog actually displays would change confidence from medium to high.

peer_identity_verified and definitions_pinned for all three MCP servers are inferred as false from the 'npx -y ...@latest' / unversioned launch pattern in mcp.json; no explicit statement of version pinning was given either way.
